results.title: Fireworks is raising on-demand GPU prices up to 30% on September 1 | Beyond the News
highlights:
# Fireworks is raising on-demand GPU prices up to 30% on September 1

Fireworks' current pricing table shows September 1 increases across H100, H200, B200, B300 and GB300 on-demand deployments, with B200 rising from $10 to $13 per GPU-hour. Dedicated training jobs that use the same GPU-hour rates inherit the new economics.

Reviewed and published by Lars Jansen Updated 28 Aug 2026, 10:59 pm NZST 4 min read Copy link

 First published 28 Aug 2026, 10:59 pm NZST 

## Key details

1. The new Fireworks on-demand GPU rates begin September 1, 2026.
2. H100 80GB: $7 → $8 per GPU-hour.
3. H200 141GB: $7 → $8 per GPU-hour.
4. B200 180GB: $10 → $13 per GPU-hour.
5. B300 288GB: $12 → $15 per GPU-hour.
6. GB300 288GB: $18 → $20 per GPU-hour.
7. On-demand deployments are billed per GPU second with no extra startup charges.
8. Region-restricted deployments are priced at a 1.5× premium.
9. Dedicated Training API jobs use the same on-demand GPU-hour pricing.

## What builders should take away

1. Update September budgets now for any persistent Fireworks deployment; the B200 and B300 changes are large enough to invalidate old monthly forecasts.
2. Benchmark cost per completed workload across H100/H200/B200/B300 rather than assuming a newer GPU is automatically cheaper after the rate changes.
3. If workload residency requires region-restricted deployment, apply the 1.5× premium after the new base rate rather than modeling only the published headline number.
4. For training, recalculate long-running jobs and experiment budgets because Dedicated Training uses the same GPU-hour table.
5. Compare dedicated deployments with Fireworks serverless and competing providers after the increase; usage shape can change which model is economically preferable.

## What changed

Fireworks' current pricing page publishes a two-column transition for its on-demand GPU deployments: prices through August 31 and new rates from September 1, 2026. H100 80GB and H200 141GB increase from $7 to $8 per GPU-hour; B200 180GB rises from $10 to $13; B300 288GB from $12 to $15; and GB300 288GB from $18 to $20. Fireworks bills on-demand deployments per GPU second with no startup charge, and its Dedicated Training API uses the same GPU-hour pricing, so the change affects both dedicated serving and GPU-hour training jobs. Region-restricted deployments continue to carry a 1.5× premium.

## Why it matters

Dedicated GPU economics can dominate the unit cost of high-volume inference, fine-tuning and reinforcement-learning workloads. These increases range from roughly 11% to 30%, large enough to change break-even points between accelerator generations, serverless APIs and competing GPU clouds. The biggest increase is on B200, where a workload consuming 1,000 GPU-hours per month moves from $10,000 to $13,000 before regional premiums or other services. Teams should therefore benchmark completed-task throughput rather than choosing hardware on hourly price or peak specifications alone.

## The September increase varies materially by accelerator

H100 and H200 move from $7 to $8 per hour, about a 14.3% increase. B200 rises 30% from $10 to $13, B300 rises 25% from $12 to $15 and GB300 rises about 11.1% from $18 to $20. The uneven changes can alter the relative cost ranking of GPUs even when performance remains unchanged.

## Training inherits the same GPU-hour table

Fireworks states that Dedicated Training API jobs are priced per GPU hour using the On-Demand Pricing section. Teams running reinforcement fine-tuning or dedicated training should therefore update both serving and training forecasts, not only inference deployment budgets.

## Per-second billing limits idle waste but not rate exposure

On-demand deployments are billed by the second and do not charge extra startup time, which remains useful for bursty workloads. But sustained fleets still absorb the full hourly increase, and a region-restricted deployment costs 1.5 times the listed rate.

## Hourly price is not total inference cost

A more expensive accelerator can still win if it materially improves throughput, latency or batch efficiency. Builders should compare cost per successful request, training run or completed agent task under the exact model, quantization, context and concurrency they use.

## What to watch next

- Whether Fireworks changes serverless model token prices alongside the dedicated GPU increases.
- Customer-facing explanations or contract options for the September pricing change.
- Reserved or committed-capacity discounts that offset the higher on-demand rates.
- Independent throughput-per-dollar comparisons on B200/B300/GB300 after the new rates take effect.

## Still unclear

- The pricing page publishes the dated rate transition but does not explain the commercial rationale for each GPU-specific increase.
- Effective cost varies significantly with model serving efficiency, batching, quantization, context length and utilization.
- Enterprise or negotiated contracts may differ from public on-demand pricing.

results.title: OVHcloud Raises Prices as AI Memory Demand Reprices Non-AI Infrastructure - InfoQ
results.author: Steef-Jan Wiggers
highlights:
OVHcloud will raise prices across most of its catalog this autumn, and the cause sits outside the products being repriced. Memory and storage costs have climbed steeply since mid-2025, and founder Octave Klaba traces that to the AI buildout pulling fabrication capacity away from the components every ordinary server is built from.

Klaba set out the mechanism in a post on X. Three global RAM suppliers have reconfigured their factories toward high-bandwidth memory, which serves GPUs and carries better margins, at the expense of standard DDR4 and DDR5. He posts in French, and the quotes here come from platform translations.

The numbers come from OVHcloud's own purchasing. Indexed to June 2025, memory reached 604 by June 2026, SSDs 323, and hard drives 148. Klaba's forecast goes further:

> This month, in June 2026, we're paying 6x the price for RAM that we paid in June 2025. We already know it will be x9 in September 2026, while forecasts for early 2027 are at x12!?

[Components inflation, indexed to June 2025 (Source: OVHcloud)]

He adds that NVMe drives are at 7x and hard drives at 3.5x, and reports hearing that CPUs, motherboards, and network cards will rise 15 to 20 percent.

The increases land unevenly. Renters of 2026-edition gaming servers face the steepest rise at 87 percent, while other recent servers go up 40 to 59 percent, all from September. Customers on 2024-era equipment see smaller increases at renewal, which Klaba puts at three to six times lower than a new order. Older ranges including Kimsufi, Rise, and earlier Advance and Scale generations are untouched, as they were in an April increase.

Some charges are also being restructured rather than raised. From October 1, storage and IP addresses become separate line items on Gen3 instances, at €0.000146 per GB per hour and €0.0027 per hour. OVHcloud is dropping its one-month, six-month, and 24-month saving plans, keeping the 12- and 36-month options that lock pricing for their duration.

Klaba is direct about how long this lasts:

> The situation is exceptional and will last until 2028. AI demand is insane at every level: datacenters, GPUs, token-as-a-service, agentic AI. Everyone wants it, everyone is using it. That's what's impacting every business that's not "AI".

...

What lifts this above a vendor pricing note is the asymmetry it exposes. Klaba described OVHcloud's purchasing position as ordering:

> month by month, over 12 months, with no guarantee of the purchase price and without knowing what will be the real demand from our customers

Amazon buys in the same market and has moved almost nothing. It raised EC2 Capacity Blocks for ML, a reserved GPU product, by roughly 20 percent in July after about 15 percent in January, and left the rest of the catalog alone, including instances running Trainium, the accelerator it designs itself. The change appeared on the pricing page with no announcement, and the company said afterward only that Capacity Blocks prices are updated periodically based on supply and demand.

...

That gap may prove temporal rather than permanent. The Register spoke to the founder of a mid-sized managed service provider who was unsurprised by the OVHcloud news and expects Azure and AWS to announce similar increases before long. Klaba hedges the same way, qualifying his own pricing claims with "if our competitors don't increase their prices."

Customer reaction on Reddit was limited but pointed, and centered less on the increase than on its frequency. Commenter bammitscamm summarized the schedule and added:

> Not happy about this, especially after just raising the prices in April.

...

If those reactions are representative, the immediate customer question isn't whether the increase is justified, but how often it recurs. Two rises inside six months turn capacity planning into a rolling negotiation, and the surviving saving plans read as OVHcloud saying so.

results.title: Cheapest H100 and B200 Cloud: CoreWeave vs Nebius vs Lambda vs Crusoe · Aliteq
results.author: Aliteq Team
highlights:
On each provider's own pricing page on Nov 3, 2026, Crusoe had the cheapest on-demand H100 ($3.90 a GPU-hour, rising to $4.50 on Dec 1) and Lambda the cheapest B200 ($6.69). CoreWeave was the most expensive on demand, but its fixed spot prices undercut everyone's on-demand rate. The full table, the catches, and where the marketplace tier sits.

...

Which big GPU cloud is cheapest for H100 and B200? On each provider's own pricing page on November 3, 2026: for the H100, Crusoe at $3.90 per GPU-hour on demand, with Lambda a cent behind at $3.99 on an 8-GPU instance. For the B200, Lambda at $6.69 per GPU-hour (8x), well under Nebius ($8.50) and CoreWeave ($8.60). CoreWeave is the most expensive on demand, but if your job can be interrupted its published spot prices ($2.46 an H100, $4.26 a B200, per GPU) undercut everyone's on-demand rate. Two dates to know: Crusoe's own page says its H100 goes to $4.50 on December 1, 2026, which hands the cheapest on-demand H100 to Lambda.

...

Among CoreWeave, Nebius, Lambda and Crusoe, the cheapest on-demand H100 on November 3, 2026 was Crusoe at $3.90 per GPU-hour, then Lambda at $3.99 (8x instance), Nebius at $4.50 and CoreWeave at $6.16 (an 8-GPU node at $49.24 an hour). Crusoe's page says its H100 rises to $4.50 on December 1, 2026. The cheapest on-demand B200 was Lambda at $6.69 per GPU-hour (8x; $6.99 on one GPU), then Nebius at $8.50 and CoreWeave at $8.60; Crusoe's B200 is contact-sales. For interruptible work, CoreWeave's spot nodes work out to $2.46 per H100 and $4.26 per B200, and Nebius preemptible starts from $0.79 (H100) and $0.99 (B200) at a dynamic rate. Smaller clouds go lower still: Hyperstack listed a B200 at $6.00 and an H100 at $2.50.

...

- H100 on demand, per GPU-hour, Nov 3, 2026: Crusoe $3.90, Lambda $3.99 (8x) to $4.29 (1x SXM), Nebius $4.50, CoreWeave $6.16.
- B200 on demand, per GPU-hour: Lambda $6.69 (8x) to $6.99 (1x), Nebius $8.50, CoreWeave $8.60, Crusoe contact sales.
- CoreWeave charges 58% more than Crusoe and 54% more than Lambda for an on-demand H100, and 29% more than Lambda for a B200 (our arithmetic from the published prices).
- Crusoe's page lists new on-demand prices starting Dec 1, 2026: H100 $3.90 to $4.50, H200 $4.29 to $5.40, B300 $8.96 to $9.90.
- CoreWeave's public prices are for whole 8-GPU nodes; Lambda's price table lists separate single-GPU (1x) prices for the H100 and B200.

...

Lambda has the lowest on-demand B200, but it lists no spot or preemptible tier. Nebius's preemptible prices ("from $0.79" for H100 and H200, "from $0.99" for B200 and B300) are floors, and Nebius says spot prices are dynamic and "may vary during the active use, including as frequently as every 15 minutes." Its live spot widget on Nov 3, 2026 showed a B200 at $5.70 in me-west1, up 39% on the week. A listed price also doesn't guarantee capacity, at any of the four.

...

- Hyperstack listed on-demand H100 at $2.50 (PCIe), $2.60 (NVLink) and $3.20 (SXM), H200 SXM at $3.99, B200 at $6.00 and B300 at $7.40 per hour on Nov 3, 2026. That B200 price is the lowest data-center on-demand B200 we found on a public price list that day.
- GMI Cloud listed H100 from $2.60 and H200 from $3.20 per GPU-hour; its B200 "from $5.00" is marked contact sales.
- Runpod (Secure Cloud pods) listed H100 PCIe at $2.89, H100 SXM at $3.99, H200 at $5.29 and B200 at $7.99 per hour. The same page's product data also lists Community Cloud rates (B200 $5.98, H100 PCIe $1.99), but its docs say "Runpod is no longer accepting new hosts for Community Cloud. Existing Community Cloud resources remain available," so that capacity is limited to the hosts already there.
- Vast.ai, a marketplace, had H100 SXM from $2.40 and H100 PCIe from $2.54 per hour on demand in our 15:20 UTC read on Nov 3, 2026. Its cheapest on-demand B200 was $10.25, more than any big cloud, so the marketplace isn't the cheap route for Blackwell right now.

results.title: Cloud GPU Price Trends 2026: Why Rates Are Rising Again
results.author: Sarthak Vaish
highlights:
> TL;DR: Cloud GPU prices are rising in 2026, not falling. H100 rental rates hit a low near $2.79/GPU-hr in mid-2025, then rose about 40% to $2.35/hr on one-year contracts by March 2026 and $2.82/hr on the spot-contract composite by April, driven by a Blackwell supply crunch (CoWoS packaging and HBM capacity) colliding with inference demand that now exceeds training demand. Expect H100/H200 rates to stay elevated or climb further through Q4 2026 as booked capacity clears; expect a real ease only once TSMC's CoWoS gap narrows toward its projected 10% by year-end and Blackwell Ultra volume lands in early 2027. Older cards (A100, V100) keep getting cheaper the whole time. That part of the trend hasn't reversed.

results.title: ISSUE #7: The B300 Trickle
results.author: Bobby Clay
highlights:
The one-line read. The four public floors did not move this week: H100 SXM $3.85, H200 $4.29, B200 $6.69, A100 SXM4 $2.30, the same levels we have shown since mid-July. Two things moved around them. The OCPI transaction index rose under three of the four floors, narrowing every gap on the board. And the B300, a chip that has been shipping since last year, is still finding a public price: only a few clouds list it on-demand, intermittently, and where they do the numbers range from about $7.85 to about $26.15 per GPU-hour. A settled floor, a firming index underneath it, and an established Blackwell GPU whose public price is still a trickle.

...

- Floors held. All four board floors are unchanged: H100 SXM $3.85 (Nebius), H200 $4.29 (Crusoe), B200 $6.69 (Lambda), A100 SXM4 $2.30 (Crusoe), the same levels we have published since mid-July. Across all nine indexed providers, no comparable public on-demand rate moved more than 1% week over week.
- The index moved under them. The floors held, but the OCPI transaction index did not. Week over week it rose for H100 ($2.64 to $2.87), B200 ($5.93 to $6.64), and A100 SXM4 ($1.02 to $1.07), and fell for H200 ($4.75 to $4.42). With the floors flat, every gap on the board narrowed. B200’s floor is now just $0.05 above the index, the tightest spread on the board.
- The B300 trickle. The B300 is an established Blackwell-generation GPU, in market since last year, with prior history in the AIForge Works catalog. What is still catching up is its public price. Only a handful of clouds list it on-demand, and they do so intermittently: AWS’s eight-GPU p6-b300.48xlarge appeared in Seoul for the first time in our reviewed history this week (Linux and four licensed operating-system variants), while Nebius listings dropped and then returned. We now see publicly listed on-demand B300 rates from three providers, AWS, OCI, and Nebius; CoreWeave shows the SKU but its rate is still contact-sales. The listed rates disagree sharply, from about $7.85 per GPU-hour (Nebius, three regions) to about $26.15 (AWS, Seoul). That is catalog visibility, not orderable capacity, and it is what a chip still finding its public price looks like.

...

The public catalog rates AIForge Works presents are on-demand and normalized to a per-GPU-hour basis unless stated otherwise. OCPI is transaction-index context, not a catalog price. Listed or indexed does not mean orderable, and neither is a live quote, an availability guarantee, or a purchase recommendation. Verify current pricing, availability, terms, and fees directly with the provider before acting.

results.title: Nvidia customers reportedly warned about AI-related price hikes
results.author: Michelle Fox
highlights:
Published Sat, Aug 22 2026 4:26 PM EDT

Michelle Fox@MFoxCNBC

Key Points

- Nvidia said it will raise prices for some of its largest customers by at least 15%, Bloomberg reported. 
- The increases are expected to take effect on systems shipped early next year.

Jensen Huang, chief executive officer of Nvidia Corp., speaks to members of the media following the company's "Japan AI Ecosystem" reception in Tokyo, Japan, on Thursday, July 16, 2026. 

Kiyoshi Ota | Bloomberg | Getty Images

Nvidia Add To Watchlist plans to hike prices for some of its largest customers, Bloomberg News reported Saturday.

The chipmaker is set to increase the cost of servers containing its artificial intelligence chips, including Vera Rubin and Grace Blackwell, by more than 15% in many cases, according to the outlet. The price gains will reportedly depend on the chip generation and memory configurations. 

Customers can expect the price increase to take effect on systems shipped next year, Bloomberg said.

Nvidia has been facing the soaring costs of memory chips, which are essential for its GPUs and systems.

results.title: Nvidia price hike will raise IT costs for all, analysts say | TechTarget
results.author: Beth Pariseau
highlights:
Nvidia price hikes are coming, company executives confirmed on an earnings call late Wednesday, and experts predict the entire tech industry -- enterprises included -- will feel the pinch.

...

Still, the company behind the mammoth Vera Rubin rack-scale AI infrastructure platform lowered its gross profit margin outlook for the remainder of its fiscal year and beyond due to "extreme pricing conditions" in the memory market, according to executive vice president and CFO Colette Kress.

"The magnitude of the price increase has exceeded our prior expectations and [is] headed even higher into next year. As a result, we are resetting expectations today," Kress said during the company's quarterly earnings call. Nvidia's future commitments to suppliers over the next three years more than doubled from the previous quarter to $279 billion, according to the company's earnings report.

The company's gross margins will decline to an estimated 74% in the fiscal third quarter, then "[hit] bottom" in the 71-72% range in the fourth quarter, Kress said. In fiscal 2028, those margins will increase again to between 72 and 73%, Kress said, "as executed price increases take effect in [fiscal] Q1" of 2028. Nvidia's fiscal 2028 will kick off at the end of January 2027.

...

These comments partially confirmed a Bloomberg report on Aug. 22 that the company's largest customers have been notified of an upcoming Nvidia price hike, but did not confirm the report's estimate that prices will rise by more than 15%.

...

Although large hyperscalers and frontier AI companies still account for most of Nvidia's direct chip customer base, enterprise IT buyers will feel the effects of the price hike -- whether or not they purchase AI infrastructure, according to industry analysts.

...

"The thing driving the increase is more the memory than the GPUs, and memory goes into just about everything, so enterprises pay twice," said Mike Leone, an analyst at Moor Insights & Strategy. "One, AI capacity costs more, and they'll feel that in cloud pricing. And two, a normal 2027 hardware refresh gets more expensive as well, on servers, storage and laptops."

...

Nvidia joins other IT infrastructure suppliers in warning of price hikes due to a global shortage of computer memory. Dell, for example, acknowledged in a November 2025 earnings call that price hikes will also be coming for customers over the next year due to memory supply constraints. Apple raised prices on consumer products due to the memory shortage in June 2026; Qualcomm notified customers of chip price hikes in July, effective Sept 1.

results.title: Nvidia to raise AI server prices by 15 percent; GPUs also becoming more expensive - ITdaily
results.author: Michaël Aussems
highlights:
Starting next year, Nvidia will increase the prices for its AI servers containing the latest accelerators by at least fifteen percent.

The increase in memory prices, caused by the AI hype partly driven by Nvidia, is now affecting Nvidia itself. Or more accurately: Nvidia’s major customers. They are receiving a warning from the company: from 2027, server prices will rise by 27 percent or more.

## Memory cost

The price increase will affect systems containing the latest chips. This includes not only the recently launched Vera Rubin systems, but also Grace Blackwell-based servers. Bloomberg reports this based on anonymous sources. Nvidia has not yet publicly communicated the price increase.

The increase is not surprising. The main culprit is the cost of memory, of which AI chips require very large quantities. The manufacturers of this memory (primarily Samsung, SK Hynix, and Micron) are prioritizing the HBM memory that AI providers need. They do this mainly because the margins are higher than on DDR memory for computers and standard servers. However, the focus on HBM is not enough to stabilize the price.

...

Prices are also rising for less specialized components. Nvidia remains the major manufacturer of GPUs, for both workstations and recreational use. These also contain memory, and those chips are becoming more expensive as well. An RTX 5070 is expected to become more than 30 percent more expensive. For these chips, too, it is not as if Nvidia was charging low prices before the increase: what was expensive is becoming even more so.
